summary: Retatrutide is a peptide in the incretin & amylin analogs class (GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptor triple agonist). Europe PMC indexes 197 publications naming it or a listed alias in a title or abstract, including 7 randomized controlled trials and 9 clinical trials of any design, as of 2026-09-14. The strongest evidence tier in that literature is human clinical trials. This page reports what those studies state, sentence by sentence, with each statement tied to its source and labeled by the kind of evidence it is. It does not recommend use, and it does not translate study doses into anything personal.

faq.question: Has Retatrutide been tested in humans?
faq.answer: Yes. Europe PMC indexes 9 clinical trials and 7 randomized controlled trials naming Retatrutide or a listed alias in the title or abstract. The evidence table above lists the ones in this record's ledger with their design and sample size; check the study name, since an alias can refer to a different formulation of the same molecule.

faq.question: What kind of evidence exists for Retatrutide?
faq.answer: The strongest tier is human clinical trial: human clinical trials. Every claim on this page carries its own tier, because a compound with one human trial and forty animal studies is described by both facts, not the better one.

faq.question: Is Retatrutide an approved medicine?
faq.answer: ChEMBL records CHEMBL5095485 at maximum clinical phase 3, with no approval recorded. Approval status differs by jurisdiction and is pending human review on this record.

faq.question: Which species has Retatrutide been studied in?
faq.answer: Studies in this record's ledger report work in: Humans, Mice, Rats. Findings in one species do not transfer to another, and weight-normalized doses in particular do not scale linearly between them.

guide.heading: Retatrutide in two minutes
guide.lede: What it is, what the best-evidenced number actually says, and what has not happened yet.
guide.html:
Retatrutide, developed as LY3437943, activates three receptors at once: the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor, the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor and the glucagon receptor. Semaglutide acts on one of those, tirzepatide on two.

No regulator has approved it, anywhere, for anything. It is an investigational molecule. Every figure on this page comes from a trial run by or for its developer, and none of those trials was a prescription.

The largest published obesity trial was phase 2: 338 adults, 48 weeks, once-weekly injection.{{cite:pmid-37366315}} At the highest dose the least-squares mean weight change was -24.2% in the 12-mg group{{cite:pmid-37366315}} against -2.1% in the placebo group{{cite:pmid-37366315}}. That number is real, and it is also a 48-week result at 12 mg in a trial of 338 people, which is a narrower claim than the way it usually travels.

A phase 3 trial in type 2 diabetes has since reported,{{cite:pmid-42250575}} and a four-trial phase 3 programme in obesity is still running.{{cite:pmid-41090431}} Both are tabled below with the registration numbers their own papers declare.

guide.heading: The registered trials, and which have reported
guide.lede: Registrations as the published papers declare them, separating trials that have results from trials that only have a design.
guide.html:

The phase 3 obesity programme, TRIUMPH, is described in a design paper rather than a results paper. It describes four phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind studies comparing weekly retatrutide injections under the skin with placebo, alongside a healthy diet and physical activity, in more than 5800 participants{{cite:pmid-41090431}}, covering obesity, obstructive sleep apnoea and knee osteoarthritis. A design paper states what a trial intends to measure. It is not a result, and nothing about weight loss in those 5,800 people can be read from it.

The phase 3 diabetes trial states that it is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT06354660 and has been completed{{cite:pmid-42250575}}.

guide.heading: What the weight-loss numbers were, dose by dose
guide.lede: The phase 2 obesity trial at both of its time points, and the phase 3 diabetes trial's blood-sugar result.
guide.html:
One trial produced the weight-loss figures that circulate: a phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 338 adults with obesity, dosed once weekly for 48 weeks.{{cite:pmid-37366315}} Both time points are given below because the primary endpoint was at 24 weeks and the number people quote is from 48.

Least-squares mean percentage change in body weight, Jastreboff 2023, n=338. Dose groups are as randomised.{{cite:pmid-37366315}}

The trial also reported how many people crossed each threshold at 48 weeks. Among those given 12 mg, 100%, 93% and 83%{{cite:pmid-37366315}} reached 5%, 10% and 15% weight reduction respectively, against 27%, 9% and 2%{{cite:pmid-37366315}} on placebo.

One finding is reported in almost no secondary coverage of this trial: heart rate rose in a dose-dependent way, peaking at 24 weeks and declining after that{{cite:pmid-37366315}}. It is in the abstract, it is dose-dependent, and it is the reason the 24-week and 48-week pictures are not the same picture.

In type 2 diabetes the phase 3 trial measured blood sugar rather than weight as its primary endpoint. Mean HbA1c change from baseline at 40 weeks was -1.69% (SE 0.11) with retatrutide 4 mg, -1.86% (0.10) with 9 mg and -1.94% (0.08) with 12 mg, compared with -0.81% (0.12) with placebo{{cite:pmid-42250575}}. Note that its dose ladder is 4, 9 and 12 mg, not the 1, 4, 8 and 12 of the obesity trial.

guide.heading: The escalation schedules the trials used
guide.lede: The starting dose changed the side-effect rate, which is why it is reported here and not only the target.
guide.html:
Nobody in either trial started at the dose they ended on, and the starting dose was not a detail. The phase 2 obesity trial randomised people to six retatrutide arms, and two of its doses were deliberately tested from two different starting points: 1 mg; 4 mg starting at 2 mg; 4 mg starting at 4 mg; 8 mg starting at 2 mg; 8 mg starting at 4 mg; or 12 mg starting at 2 mg{{cite:pmid-37366315}}.

That design existed to answer a question about tolerability, and it did. Gastrointestinal events were related to dose, mostly mild to moderate in severity, and partly reduced by a lower starting dose (2 mg vs. 4 mg){{cite:pmid-37366315}}. The same target dose was easier to tolerate when approached from 2 mg than from 4 mg.

A dose chart that lists only target doses has therefore dropped the variable the trial was built to test.

guide.heading: Common mistakes in how retatrutide is discussed
guide.lede: Each of these appears on a page currently ranking for this compound.
guide.html:
Four things go wrong repeatedly in how this molecule is written about, and all four are visible in the pages currently ranking for it.

  • Quoting -24.2% as retatrutide's weight loss. It is the 48-week least-squares mean at 12 mg in a 338-person phase 2 trial. At 24 weeks the same group was at -17.5%, and at 1 mg the 48-week figure was -8.7%.{{cite:pmid-37366315}}
  • Treating a phase 3 registration as a result. The obesity programme is described in a design paper.{{cite:pmid-41090431}} A trial that has enrolled 5,800 people has not thereby reported anything.
  • Printing 12 mg as a dose to take. In the trial it was a target reached by escalation from 2 mg, under supervision, with dropout and adverse events recorded.{{cite:pmid-37366315}}
  • Comparing the headline number to tirzepatide's or semaglutide's. Different trials, different durations, different populations and different endpoints. The arithmetic looks like a comparison and is not one.
